Hayashi Property for Conjugation Quandles

.

Filip Filipi

.

Department of Algebra

Faculty of Mathematics and Physics

Sokolovská 83, Praha 8, Prague, 186 75, Czech Republic

filip.filipi@matfyz.cuni.cz

Abstract

We give a comprehensive description of conjugation quandles and their connectedness. In this context, we find a characterization of Hayashi’s conjecture (2013) in terms of a centrality condition of groups. This condition is thus a conjecture itself and it states that powers of elements of a finite and generating conjugacy classes should be central whenever they commute with one particular element of this class. We prove this condition in several cases, e.g. for finite nilpotent, symmetric, alternating, and dihedral groups. All of these results translate to Hayashi’s conjecture for the corresponding conjugation quandles.
.
Keywords: Hayashi’s conjecture; quandle; conjugation; conjugacy class; group.
MSC2020: 20E34, 20E45, 20N02, 57K12.

1 Introduction

An algebraic structure called quandle arises naturally in knot theory. The axioms of this structure are based on the Reidemeister moves. Those are a complete collection of knot diagram manipulations needed to decide whether two diagrams represent the same knot. Using a notion of proper knot diagram colorings, this allows quandles to define an invariant useful in distinguishing (oriented) knots by their diagrams. To those interested in the origin and motivation of quandles, we recommend reading the introductory section of [1] by Fish, Lisitsa & Stanovský, which explains all this in a comprehensive yet concise manner. More complete basic knowledge and concepts from knot theory can be found in the book Quandles [2] by Elhamdadi & Nelson.

As stated in Section 5.2 of [3], if two knots can be distinguished by a quandle, then they can also be distinguished by one of its connected subquandles. A structural restriction for finite connected quandles has been conjectured by Hayashi in 2013 [4]. This conjecture has been further studied in [5, 6, 7, 8, 9], and it was pointed out in [10] that the results of [11] also contribute to it. For a family of so called conjugation quandles, this conjecture still remains open.

This work completes Kayacan’s ideas that first appeared in an arXiv paper [8] in 2021 and provides more accessible proofs and generalizations of some of his claims in the process. We introduce a notion of a Hayashi property and in Proposition 4.1, we characterize it in terms of a structural property of groups. This especially applies to Hayashi’s conjecture for connected conjugation quandles and motivates Conjecture 4.1 claiming that for some group elements, the property of being central might actually be witnessed on a single element of this group. Moreover, we study this property in a greater context provided by Problem 5.1 and we decide it for 𝐒n,𝐀n,𝐃2​n\mathbf{S}_{n},\mathbf{A}_{n},\mathbf{D}_{2n}, finite nilpotent groups, simple non-abelian groups of order ≤3.500.000\leq 3.500.000, and general groups of order ≤500\leq 500. These results especially translate to proofs of Hayashi’s conjecture for particular conjugation quandles.

2 Preliminaries

Most of the terminology used is based on [12] written by Cvrček & Stanovský.

Notation. Let there be a set QQ. Given a subgroup 𝐇\mathbf{H} of the symmetric group 𝐒Q\mathbf{S}_{Q}, we denote 𝐇z\mathbf{H}_{z}, the stabilizer subgroup of 𝐇\mathbf{H} with respect to z∈Qz\in Q, that is, Hz={f∈𝐒Q∣f⁡(z)=z}H_{z}=\{f\in\mathbf{S}_{Q}\mid f(z)=z\}.

Notation. Given a group 𝐆\mathbf{G} and its element gg, by ϕg\phi_{g} we denote the (left) conjugation by an element gg in the group GG, that is, ϕg:G→G,x↦g​x​g−1\phi_{g}:G\to G,\ x\mapsto gxg^{-1}. Such a mapping is an automorphism of 𝐆\mathbf{G}, and a set of all such maps form the inner automorphism group of 𝐆\mathbf{G}, denoted by Inn⁡(𝐆)≤𝐒G\operatorname{Inn}\left(\mathbf{G}\right)\leq\mathbf{S}_{G}. For an element hh of a subgroup 𝐇≤𝐆\mathbf{H}\leq\mathbf{G}, it should be clear from the context whether the domain of ϕh\phi_{h} is considered to be HH or GG.

Notation. Given a group 𝐆\mathbf{G} and its element zz, we denote C𝐆⁡(z):={g∈G∣g​z=z​g}≤𝐆\operatorname{C}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(z\right):=\{g\in G\mid gz=zg\}\leq\mathbf{G}, the centralizer of zz in the group 𝐆\mathbf{G}.

Definition 2.1.

Let QQ be a finite nonempty set and π∈SQ\pi\in S_{Q}, we say that (λ1α1,…,λtαt)(\lambda_{1}^{\alpha_{1}},\dots,\lambda_{t}^{\alpha_{t}}) is a cycle structure11 1 or profile of a permutation π\pi if the following conditions are satisfied

  • •

    λ1⪇λ2⪇⋯⪇λt\lambda_{1}\lneq\lambda_{2}\lneq\dots\lneq\lambda_{t},

  • •

    for every i∈{1,…,t}i\in\{1,\dots,t\}, αi∈ℕ\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{N} is the number of cycles of length λi\lambda_{i} in π\pi,

  • •

    each cycle is counted, that is ∑i=1tαi⋅λi=|Q|\sum_{i=1}^{t}\alpha_{i}\cdot\lambda_{i}=\left|Q\right|.

As long as QQ is finite, it always exists, is uniquely defined, and is preserved upon conjugation by elements of SQS_{Q}. Furthermore, if it holds that λi|λt\lambda_{i}\mid\lambda_{t} for all i∈{1,…,t}i\in\{1,\dots,t\}, we say that the permutation π\pi contains a regular cycle.

Remark. Whenever x∈Qx\in Q is an element of a cycle of length λ\lambda in π∈SQ\pi\in S_{Q}, then λ\lambda equals the smallest k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that πk​(x)=x\pi^{k}(x)=x.

Definition 2.2.

Let QQ be a nonempty set and ⋆\star a binary operation on it, then 𝐐=(Q,⋆)\mathbf{Q}=(Q,\star) is called a quandle if for each a∈Qa\in Q it holds a⋆a=aa\star a=a and the left translation22 2 one might encounter dual definition of a quandle using right translations

La:Q→Q,x↦a⋆xL_{a}:Q\to Q,\ x\mapsto a\star x

is an automorphism of 𝐐\mathbf{Q}.

We denote LMlt⁡(𝐐):=⟨La∣a∈Q⟩≤𝐒Q\operatorname{LMlt\left(\mathbf{Q}\right)}:=\left<L_{a}\mid a\in Q\right>\leq\mathbf{S}_{Q} the (left) multiplication group of a quandle 𝐐\mathbf{Q} and we say 𝐐\mathbf{Q} is connected33 3 or indecomposable if LMlt⁡(𝐐)\operatorname{LMlt\left(\mathbf{Q}\right)} acts transitively on QQ, i.e., for any a,b∈Qa,b\in Q there is φ∈LMlt⁡(𝐐)\varphi\in\operatorname{LMlt\left(\mathbf{Q}\right)} such that b=φ⁡(a)b=\varphi(a).

It is useful to introduce the following property of quandles.

Definition 2.3.

We say that a quandle 𝐐\mathbf{Q} has a Hayashi property if all of its left translations contain a regular cycle.

Using it, we may now state a conjecture proposed in [4] as follows.

Conjecture 2.1 (Hayashi, 2013).

Finite connected quandles have the Hayashi property.

Given a quandle automorphism α\alpha and a,xa,x elements of its ground set,

Lα⁡(a)​(x)=α⁡(a)⋆x=α⁡(a⋆α−1​(x))=α∘La∘α−1​(x).L_{\alpha(a)}(x)=\alpha(a)\star x=\alpha(a\star\alpha^{-1}(x))=\alpha\circ L_{a}\circ\alpha^{-1}(x). (1)

In connected quandles, for any two left translations La,LbL_{a},L_{b}, there is a quandle automorphism φ\varphi such that b=φ⁡(a)b=\varphi(a). Due to Eq. 1, it holds that Lb=Lφ⁡(a)=φ∘La∘φ−1L_{b}=L_{\varphi(a)}=\varphi\circ L_{a}\circ\varphi^{-1}, and so they have the same cycle structure. This shows that connected quandle has the Hayashi property if and only if at least one of its left translations contains a regular cycle.

3 Conjugation Quandles and their Connectedness

We now define a special type of a quandle which is related to groups. This shall be the main object studied in this paper.

Definition 3.1.

Let 𝐆\mathbf{G} be a group and 𝐂:=(C,⋆)\mathbf{C}:=(C,\star) a quandle. If C⊆GC\subseteq G and a⋆b=a​b​a−1a\star b=aba^{-1} for each a,b∈Ca,b\in C, then we say 𝐂\mathbf{C} is a conjugation quandle over the group 𝐆\mathbf{G}.

Description of conjugation quandles seems to be well known, but since we could not find any references, we derive it ourselves. The following lemma is a simple observation which will be used with no further mentions.

Lemma 3.1.

Let 𝐂\mathbf{C} be a conjugation quandle over a group 𝐆\mathbf{G}. Then

  1. 1.

    for any c∈Cc\in C it holds Lc=ϕc↾CL_{c}=\phi_{c}\restriction_{C} and Lc−1=ϕc−1↾CL_{c}^{-1}=\phi_{c^{-1}}\restriction_{C},

  2. 2.

    LMlt⁡(𝐂)=Inn(⟨C⟩)↾C\operatorname{LMlt\left(\mathbf{C}\right)}=\operatorname{Inn}\left(\left<C\right>\right)\restriction_{C} as groups.

Proof.
  1. (1)

    First part is given by the definition of the quandle operation of 𝐂\mathbf{C}. To prove the second part, observe that

    ϕc−1↾C∘Lc=ϕc−1↾C∘ϕc↾C=idC,\phi_{c^{-1}}\restriction_{C}\circ L_{c}=\phi_{c^{-1}}\restriction_{C}\circ\phi_{c}\restriction_{C}=\operatorname{id}_{C},

    and since we know LcL_{c} is a bijection, ϕc−1↾C\phi_{c^{-1}}\restriction_{C} has to be its both-sided inverse.

  2. (2)

    According to (1),

    LMlt⁡(𝐂)=⟨{Lc∣c∈C}⟩=⟨{ϕc↾C∣c∈C}⟩.\operatorname{LMlt\left(\mathbf{C}\right)}=\left<\{L_{c}\mid c\in C\}\right>=\left<\{\phi_{c}\restriction_{C}\mid c\in C\}\right>.

    Since it holds that ϕc↾C∘ϕc′↾C=ϕc​c′↾C\phi_{c}\restriction_{C}\circ\phi_{c^{\prime}}\restriction_{C}=\phi_{cc^{\prime}}\restriction_{C} and (ϕc↾C)−1=ϕc−1↾C(\phi_{c}\restriction_{C})^{-1}=\phi_{c^{-1}}\restriction_{C}, we additionally deduce

    ⟨{ϕc↾C∣c∈C}⟩={ϕh↾C∣h∈⟨C⟩}=Inn(⟨C⟩)↾C.\left<\{\phi_{c}\restriction_{C}\mid c\in C\}\right>=\left\{\phi_{h}\restriction_{C}\mid h\in\left<C\right>\right\}=\operatorname{Inn}\left(\left<C\right>\right)\restriction_{C}.

∎

Theorem 3.1.

Let 𝐆\mathbf{G} be a group and C⊆GC\subseteq G. Then TFAE

  1. 1.

    there is a conjugation quandle over the group 𝐆\mathbf{G} on CC,

  2. 2.

    CC is nonempty and closed upon conjugation by elements of ⟨C⟩\left<C\right>,

  3. 3.

    CC is a nonempty union of conjugacy classes of the group ⟨C⟩\left<C\right>.

Proof.

(1)⇒\Rightarrow(2): Let 𝐂:=(C,⋆)\mathbf{C}:=(C,\star) be a conjugation quandle over 𝐆\mathbf{G}. For any c,a∈Cc,a\in C it holds that c​a​c−1=c⋆a∈Ccac^{-1}=c\star a\in C and c−1ac=ϕc−1↾C(a)=Lc−1(a)∈Cc^{-1}ac=\phi_{c^{-1}}\restriction_{C}(a)=L_{c}^{-1}(a)\in C, so CC is closed upon conjugation by elements of CC and their inverses. Since it is also closed upon conjugation by products, it has to be closed upon conjugation by elements of ⟨C⟩\left<C\right>.

(2)⇒\Rightarrow(1): For any a,b,c∈Ca,b,c\in C let a⋆b:=aba−1=ϕa↾C(b)∈Ca\star b:=aba^{-1}=\phi_{a}\restriction_{C}(b)\in C. It holds that a⋆a=a​a​a−1=aa\star a=aaa^{-1}=a, and since a−1∈⟨C⟩a^{-1}\in\left<C\right>, there is a well-defined map ϕa−1↾C:C→C\phi_{a^{-1}}\restriction_{C}:C\to C inverse to La=ϕa↾CL_{a}=\phi_{a}\restriction_{C}. We now finish by proving that LaL_{a} is also a homomorphism:

La(b⋆c)=ϕa↾C(bcb−1)=ϕa↾C(b)ϕa↾C(c)ϕa↾C(b)−1\displaystyle L_{a}(b\star c)=\phi_{a}\restriction_{C}(bcb^{-1})=\phi_{a}\restriction_{C}(b)\phi_{a}\restriction_{C}(c)\phi_{a}\restriction_{C}(b)^{-1}
=La​(b)​La​(c)​La​(b)−1=La​(b)⋆La​(c).\displaystyle=L_{a}(b)L_{a}(c)L_{a}(b)^{-1}=L_{a}(b)\star L_{a}(c).

(2)⇒\Rightarrow(3): Since CC is closed upon conjugation by elements of the group ⟨C⟩\left<C\right>, C=⋃c∈C{h​c​h−1∣h∈⟨C⟩}C=\bigcup_{c\in C}\{hch^{-1}\mid h\in\left<C\right>\} is a union of conjugacy classes of ⟨C⟩\left<C\right>.

(3)⇒\Rightarrow(2): Conjugacy classes of the group ⟨C⟩\left<C\right> are closed upon conjugation by elements of ⟨C⟩\left<C\right>, and such a property is preserved upon unions. ∎

We may also note that CC and 𝐆\mathbf{G} define such conjugation quandle uniquely. On the other hand, when 𝐂\mathbf{C} is a conjugation quandle over a group 𝐆\mathbf{G}, then the same quandle is realized over the group 𝐇:=⟨C⟩\mathbf{H}:=\left<C\right>. Theorem 3.1 especially says that for a group 𝐆\mathbf{G} and its element ee, there is a conjugation quandle over 𝐆\mathbf{G} on the conjugacy class Cl𝐆⁡(e):={g​e​g−1∣g∈G}\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right):=\{geg^{-1}\mid g\in G\}. This quandle shall be denoted 𝐂𝐥𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right).

Theorem 3.2.

Let 𝐂\mathbf{C} be a conjugation quandle over a group 𝐆\mathbf{G}, then TFAE

    quandle 𝐂\mathbf{C} is connected,

  2. 2.

    CC is a conjugacy class of the group ⟨C⟩\left<C\right>.

Proof.

(1)⇒\Rightarrow(2): We may pick e∈Ce\in C. Due to Theorem 3.1, CC is a union of conjugacy classes of ⟨C⟩\left<C\right>, and so Cl⟨C⟩⁡(e)⊆C\operatorname{Cl}_{\left<C\right>}\left(e\right)\subseteq C. Since 𝐂\mathbf{C} is connected, there is φ∈LMlt⁡(𝐂)\varphi\in\operatorname{LMlt\left(\mathbf{C}\right)} such that c=φ⁡(e)c=\varphi(e). Using the equality LMlt⁡(𝐂)=Inn(⟨C⟩)↾C\operatorname{LMlt\left(\mathbf{C}\right)}=\operatorname{Inn}\left(\left<C\right>\right)\restriction_{C}, there is h∈⟨C⟩h\in\left<C\right> such that

c=φ(e)=ϕh↾C(e)=ϕh(e)∈Cl⟨C⟩(e).c=\varphi(e)=\phi_{h}\restriction_{C}(e)=\phi_{h}(e)\in\operatorname{Cl}_{\left<C\right>}\left(e\right).

(2)⇒\Rightarrow(1): Pick e∈Ce\in C. It is enough to show that for any c∈Cc\in C, there is ψ∈LMlt⁡(𝐂)\psi\in\operatorname{LMlt\left(\mathbf{C}\right)} for which c=ψ⁡(e)c=\psi(e): then for any a,b∈Ca,b\in C, there are ψ1,ψ2∈LMlt⁡(𝐂)\psi_{1},\psi_{2}\in\operatorname{LMlt\left(\mathbf{C}\right)} such that a=ψ1​(e)a=\psi_{1}(e) and b=ψ2​(e)b=\psi_{2}(e); thus, b=ψ2∘ψ1−1​(a)b=\psi_{2}\circ\psi_{1}^{-1}(a).

For a given c∈C=Cl⟨𝐂⟩⁡(e)c\in C=\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{\left<C\right>}}\left(e\right), there is h∈⟨C⟩h\in\left<C\right> such that c=ϕh​(e)c=\phi_{h}(e). Using generators, we may express hh in the form Πi=1n​cisi\Pi_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}^{s_{i}} for some n∈ℕ,ci∈C,si∈{±1}n\in\mathbb{N},c_{i}\in C,s_{i}\in\{\pm 1\} to obtain

c=ϕΠi=1n​cisi(e)=ϕc1s1∘⋯∘ϕcnsn(e)=ϕc1s1↾C∘⋯∘ϕcnsn↾C(e)\displaystyle c=\phi_{\Pi_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}^{s_{i}}}(e)=\phi_{{c_{1}}^{s_{1}}}\circ\cdots\circ\phi_{{c_{n}}^{s_{n}}}(e)=\phi_{{c_{1}}^{s_{1}}}\restriction_{C}\circ\cdots\circ\phi_{{c_{n}}^{s_{n}}}\restriction_{C}(e)
=Lc1s1∘⋯∘Lcnsn(e).\displaystyle=L_{c_{1}}^{s_{1}}\circ\cdots\circ L_{c_{n}}^{s_{n}}(e).

∎

Corollary 3.1.

Given an element ee of a simple group 𝐆\mathbf{G}, the quandle 𝐂𝐥G⁡(e)\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{G}\left(e\right) is connected.

Proof.

The subgroup ⟨Cl𝐆⁡(e)⟩\left<\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right)\right> is normal in 𝐆\mathbf{G}. If the quandle contains at least two elements, then ⟨Cl𝐆⁡(e)⟩=𝐆\left<\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right)\right>=\mathbf{G}, and by Theorem 3.2, it is connected. Otherwise, it has only one element, and so it is connected trivially. ∎

In the paper, quandles of the form 𝐂𝐥𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) occur. Be warned that despite Theorem 3.2 being an equivalence, it is possible for such quandles to not be connected when a condition 𝐆=⟨Cl𝐆⁡(C)⟩\mathbf{G}=\left<\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(C\right)\right> is not met. To show this is really the case, in Example 3.1, we prove that the conjugacy class of 𝐆\mathbf{G} may or may not split into more conjugacy classes of its subgroup ⟨Cl𝐆⁡(C)⟩\left<\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(C\right)\right>. Nevertheless, even in the not connected conjugation quandles representable as 𝐂𝐥𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right), all the left translations have the same cycle structure: for any c,c′∈Cl𝐆⁡(e)c,c^{\prime}\in\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) there is g∈Gg\in G such that c′=ϕg​(c)c^{\prime}=\phi_{g}(c). It can be verified that the map ϕ′:=ϕg↾Cl𝐆⁡(e)\phi^{\prime}:=\phi_{g}\restriction_{\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right)} is a bijection on Cl𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right), and since ϕ′​(a⋆b)=ϕg​(a​b​a−1)=ϕg​(a)​ϕg​(b)​ϕg​(a)−1=ϕ′​(a)⋆ϕ′​(b)\phi^{\prime}(a\star b)=\phi_{g}(aba^{-1})=\phi_{g}(a)\phi_{g}(b)\phi_{g}(a)^{-1}=\phi^{\prime}(a)\star\phi^{\prime}(b), it is an automorphism of 𝐂𝐥𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right). Thus, Lc′=Lϕ′​(c)=ϕ′∘Lc∘(ϕ′)−1L_{c^{\prime}}=L_{\phi^{\prime}(c)}=\phi^{\prime}\circ L_{c}\circ(\phi^{\prime})^{-1} by Eq. 1.

Example 3.1.

Recall that in 𝐒n\mathbf{S}_{n}, permutations are conjugate if and only if they have the same cycle structure, and that for n≥3n\geq 3, the alternating group 𝐀n\mathbf{A}_{n} is generated by its subset of all 33-cycles. The conjugation quandle 𝐂𝐥𝐒5⁡((1 2 3))\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{S}_{5}}\left((1\ 2\ 3)\right) is connected because ⟨Cl𝐒5⁡((1 2 3))⟩=𝐀5\left<\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{S}_{5}}\left((1\ 2\ 3)\right)\right>=\mathbf{A}_{5}, and the conjugacy class Cl𝐒5⁡((1 2 3))=Cl𝐀5⁡((1 2 3))\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{S}_{5}}\left((1\ 2\ 3)\right)=\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{A}_{5}}\left((1\ 2\ 3)\right) does not split. On the other hand, 𝐂𝐥𝐒4⁡((1 2 3))\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{S}_{4}}\left((1\ 2\ 3)\right) is not connected, since ⟨Cl𝐒4⁡((1 2 3))⟩=𝐀4\left<\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{S}_{4}}\left((1\ 2\ 3)\right)\right>=\mathbf{A}_{4} and the conjugacy class Cl𝐒4⁡((1 2 3))=Cl𝐀4⁡((1 2 3))​∪˙​Cl𝐀4⁡((1 3 2))\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{S}_{4}}\left((1\ 2\ 3)\right)=\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{A}_{4}}\left((1\ 2\ 3)\right)\dot{\cup}\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{A}_{4}}\left((1\ 3\ 2)\right) splits.

4 Regular Cycles of Left Translations

In this section, we will study what it means for a left translation to have a regular cycle in conjugation quandles. We will be able to find a complete characterization based on the structure of the defining group.

Lemma 4.1.

If 𝐐\mathbf{Q} is a finite quandle and π∈LMlt⁡(𝐐)\pi\in\operatorname{LMlt\left(\mathbf{Q}\right)}, then TFAE

  1. 1.

    permutation π\pi contains a regular cycle,

  2. 2.

    there is z∈Qz\in Q such that (⟨π⟩)z=𝟏\left(\left<\pi\right>\right)_{z}=\mathbf{1}.

Proof.

(1)⇒\Rightarrow(2): If we choose z∈Qz\in Q to be from any of the longest (regular) cycles of π\pi, then πk​(z)=z\pi^{k}(z)=z already implies πk=id\pi^{k}=\operatorname{id}.

(2)⇒\Rightarrow(1): Let ℓ\ell be the length of the cycle of such zz in π\pi. If aa is an element of any other cycle, then its length divides ℓ\ell because πℓ​(a)=id⁡(a)=a\pi^{\ell}(a)=\operatorname{id}(a)=a. ∎

The following is a part of Lemma 1.9. from [13].

Lemma 4.2.

Let 𝐂\mathbf{C} be a conjugation quandle over a group 𝐆\mathbf{G}. If we denote 𝐇:=⟨C⟩\mathbf{H}:=\left<C\right>, then there is a group isomorphism

ψ:𝐇/Z⁡(𝐇)→Inn(𝐇)↾C=LMlt⁡(𝐂),\displaystyle\psi:{\raisebox{2.04439pt}{$\mathbf{H}$}\left/\raisebox{-2.04439pt}{$\operatorname{Z}(\mathbf{H})$}\right.}\to\operatorname{Inn}\left(\mathbf{H}\right)\restriction_{C}=\operatorname{LMlt\left(\mathbf{C}\right)},
hZ(𝐇)↦ϕh↾C.\displaystyle h\operatorname{Z}(\mathbf{H})\mapsto\phi_{h}\restriction_{C}.
Proof.

The map ψ′:𝐇→Inn(𝐇)↾C\psi^{\prime}:\mathbf{H}\to\operatorname{Inn}\left(\mathbf{H}\right)\restriction_{C} defined by h↦ϕh↾Ch\mapsto\phi_{h}\restriction_{C} is a surjective group homomorphism. It holds that h∈Ker⁡(ψ′)h\in\operatorname{Ker}(\psi^{\prime}) if and only if h∈Hh\in H commutes with every element of CC. The latter happens if and only if it commutes with every element of ⟨C⟩=𝐇\left<C\right>=\mathbf{H} ; thus, Ker⁡(ψ′)=Z⁡(𝐇)\operatorname{Ker}(\psi^{\prime})=\operatorname{Z}(\mathbf{H}). By the first isomorphism theorem, there is an induced isomorphism ψ:𝐇/Z⁡(𝐇)→Inn(𝐇)↾C\psi:{\raisebox{1.99997pt}{$\mathbf{H}$}\left/\raisebox{-1.99997pt}{$\operatorname{Z}(\mathbf{H})$}\right.}\to\operatorname{Inn}\left(\mathbf{H}\right)\restriction_{C} such that hZ(𝐇)↦ϕh↾Ch\operatorname{Z}(\mathbf{H})\mapsto\phi_{h}\restriction_{C}.

∎

The preceding two lemmas serve to prove the following proposition.

Proposition 4.1.

If 𝐂\mathbf{C} is a finite conjugation quandle over a group 𝐆\mathbf{G}, and we denote 𝐇:=⟨C⟩\mathbf{H}:=\left<C\right>, then for any c∈Cc\in C, TFAE

  1. 1.

    LcL_{c} in 𝐂\mathbf{C} contains a regular cycle,

  2. 2.

    there is z∈Cz\in C such that ⟨c⟩∩C𝐇⁡(z)≤Z⁡(𝐇)\left<c\right>\cap\operatorname{C}_{\mathbf{H}}\left(z\right)\leq\operatorname{Z}(\mathbf{H}).

Proof.

By Lemma 4.1, LcL_{c} contains a regular cycle if and only if there is z∈Cz\in C such that (⟨Lc⟩)z=𝟏\left(\left<L_{c}\right>\right)_{z}=\mathbf{1}. This happens if and only if there is z∈Cz\in C such that ψ−1​((⟨Lc⟩)z)=𝟏\psi^{-1}\left(\left(\left<L_{c}\right>\right)_{z}\right)=\mathbf{1}, i.e., ∅≠⟨c⟩∩C𝐇⁡(z)≤Z⁡(𝐇)\emptyset\neq\left<c\right>\cap\operatorname{C}_{\mathbf{H}}\left(z\right)\leq\operatorname{Z}(\mathbf{H}). ∎

Corollary 4.1.

Let ee be an element of a group 𝐆\mathbf{G} such that the quandle 𝐂𝐥𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) is finite. If we denote 𝐇:=⟨Cl𝐆⁡(e)⟩\mathbf{H}:=\left<\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right)\right>, then TFAE

  1. 1.

    there is a left translation in 𝐂𝐥𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) containing a regular cycle,

  2. 2.

    there are c,z∈Cl𝐆⁡(e)c,z\in\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) such that ⟨c⟩∩C𝐇⁡(z)≤Z⁡(𝐇)\left<c\right>\cap\operatorname{C}_{\mathbf{H}}\left(z\right)\leq\operatorname{Z}(\mathbf{H}),

  3. 3.

    for every c∈Cl𝐆⁡(e)c\in\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) there is z∈Cl𝐆⁡(e)z\in\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) such that ⟨c⟩∩C𝐇⁡(z)≤Z⁡(𝐇)\left<c\right>\cap\operatorname{C}_{\mathbf{H}}\left(z\right)\leq\operatorname{Z}(\mathbf{H}),

  4. 4.

    quandle 𝐂𝐥𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) has the Hayashi property.

Proof.

We have observed in the last paragraph of Section 3 that (1)⇔\Leftrightarrow(4). Follow up by applying Proposition 4.1 to get (1)⇔\Leftrightarrow(2) and (3)⇔\Leftrightarrow(4). ∎

Remark. Proving (2)⇒\Rightarrow(3) using construction can be a nice exercise. Provided that there is one such pair c,z∈Cl𝐆⁡(e)c,z\in\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right), for given c′=ϕg​(c)∈Cl𝐆⁡(e)c^{\prime}=\phi_{g}(c)\in\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right), we show that if (c′)k∈C𝐇⁡(ϕg​(z))(c^{\prime})^{k}\in\operatorname{C}_{\mathbf{H}}\left(\phi_{g}(z)\right), then ck∈⟨c⟩∩C𝐇⁡(z)⊆Z⁡(𝐇)c^{k}\in\left<c\right>\cap\operatorname{C}_{\mathbf{H}}\left(z\right)\subseteq\operatorname{Z}(\mathbf{H}). Using the normality of ⟨C⟩\left<C\right> and the centrality of ckc^{k}, it can now be verified that (c′)k∈Z⁡(𝐇)(c^{\prime})^{k}\in\operatorname{Z}(\mathbf{H}), and so we see that we can put z′:=ϕg​(z)z^{\prime}:=\phi_{g}(z).

For brevity, we introduce a new property.

Definition 4.1.

We say that a finite conjugacy class CC of a group 𝐆\mathbf{G} is good in 𝐆\mathbf{G} if for every c∈Cc\in C there is z∈Cz\in C such that ⟨c⟩∩C𝐆⁡(z)≤Z⁡(⟨C⟩)\left<c\right>\cap\operatorname{C}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(z\right)\leq\operatorname{Z}(\left<C\right>). Moreover, we say that the group 𝐆\mathbf{G} is good if all of its finite conjugacy classes are good.

By Theorem 3.2, every connected quandle over a group 𝐆\mathbf{G} is of the form 𝐂𝐥𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right). So, in the provided terminology, Corollary 4.1 especially says the following.

Corollary 4.2.

If 𝐆\mathbf{G} is a good group, then every finite quandle of the form Cl𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) has the Hayashi property. In that case, all connected conjugation quandles over the group 𝐆\mathbf{G} satisfy Hayashi’s conjecture (Conjecture 2.1).

This can be refined to an equivalence.

Theorem 4.1.

The following conditions are equivalent

  1. 1.

    Hayashi’s conjecture (Conjecture 2.1) holds for all connected conjugation quandles,

  2. 2.

    for every group 𝐆\mathbf{G} and its finite conjugacy class CC, if ⟨C⟩=𝐆\left<C\right>=\mathbf{G}, then CC is good in 𝐆\mathbf{G}.

Proof.

(1)⇒\Rightarrow(2): Let 𝐆\mathbf{G} be a group and Cl𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) a finite conjugacy class satisfying ⟨Cl𝐆⁡(e)⟩=𝐆\left<\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right)\right>=\mathbf{G}. Using Theorem 3.2, the conjugation quandle 𝐂𝐥𝐆⁡(e)\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) is connected; thus, by (1), it has the Hayashi property. Since 𝐇:=⟨Cl𝐆⁡(e)⟩=𝐆\mathbf{H}:=\left<\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right)\right>=\mathbf{G}, Corollary 4.1 applies and finishes the proof.

(2)⇒\Rightarrow(1): Given a finite connected conjugation quandle 𝐂\mathbf{C} over a group 𝐆~\mathbf{\tilde{G}}, we denote 𝐆:=⟨C⟩\mathbf{G}:=\left<C\right>. By Theorem 3.2, C=Cl𝐆⁡(e)C=\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right) for some element e∈Ge\in G. Since we now see that 𝐂=𝐂𝐥𝐆⁡(e)\mathbf{C}=\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right), we may apply Corollary 4.1 with 𝐇:=⟨Cl𝐆⁡(e)⟩=𝐆\mathbf{H}:=\left<\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{G}}\left(e\right)\right>=\mathbf{G} to get that 𝐂\mathbf{C} has the Hayashi property. ∎

Since (1) from Theorem 4.1 is conjectured, the proposition (2) is a conjecture on its own.

Conjecture 4.1.

Let 𝐆\mathbf{G} be a group and CC its finite conjugacy class such that ⟨C⟩=𝐆\left<C\right>=\mathbf{G}. Then for any c∈Cc\in C, there exists some z∈Cz\in C such that for all k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}, the element ckc^{k} is central if and only if it commutes with zz.

As a consequence of the following section, this we have verified for all finite nilpotent groups, for the groups 𝐒n,𝐀n,𝐃2​n\mathbf{S}_{n},\mathbf{A}_{n},\mathbf{D}_{2n}, for all group of order ≤500\leq 500, and for all simple groups of order ≤3.500.000\leq 3.500.000. These results translate to Hayashi’s conjecture whenever the condition ⟨C⟩=𝐆\left<C\right>=\mathbf{G} is satisfied. Since ⟨C⟩\left<C\right> is normal in 𝐆\mathbf{G}, this generating condition is, in particular, satisfied by all nontrivial finite classes of simple groups.

5 Special cases

In this section, we focus on applying the developed theory to 𝐒n,𝐀n,𝐃2​n\mathbf{S}_{n},\mathbf{A}_{n},\mathbf{D}_{2n}, finite nilpotent groups and some groups of small orders. Since we know the correspondence given by Corollary 4.1, we may approach these problems from both, the perspective of quandles, and the perspective of groups. For example, the following lemma may be considered a use of the quandle approach in verifying that group conditions from Corollary 4.1 are satisfied for any pp-group.

Proposition 5.1.

Let 𝐂\mathbf{C} be a finite conjugation quandle over a group 𝐆\mathbf{G}. If the order of c∈Cc\in C in 𝐆\mathbf{G} is a prime power (or 11), then the left translation LcL_{c} in 𝐂\mathbf{C} contains a regular cycle.

Proof.

Let cc be of order pkp^{k} for a prime number pp and k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. Since Lc(pk)=ϕc(pk)↾C=ϕ1↾C=1L_{c}^{(p^{k})}=\phi_{c^{(p^{k})}}\restriction_{C}=\phi_{1}\restriction_{C}=1, we know that the order of LcL_{c} divides pkp^{k}; thus, cycle lengths of LcL_{c} are powers of pp and all of them divide the largest one. ∎

Direct product of finite conjugation quandles is again a finite conjugation quandle over the direct product of their defining groups. The following holds.

Proposition 5.2.

Let 𝐂1\mathbf{C}_{1} and 𝐂2\mathbf{C}_{2} be finite conjugation quandles. If 𝐂1\mathbf{C}_{1} and 𝐂2\mathbf{C}_{2} have the Hayashi property, then the direct product 𝐂1×𝐂2\mathbf{C}_{1}\times\mathbf{C}_{2} has the Hayashi property.

Proof.

Let L(c1,c2)L_{(c_{1},c_{2})} be a left translation. In general, the length of the cycle of (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}) in Lc1,c2L_{c_{1},c_{2}} equals the least common multiple of the lengths of the cycles of x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} in Lc1L_{c_{1}} and Lc2L_{c_{2}}, respectively. Pick elements z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} from any of the longest (regular) cycles of Lc1L_{c_{1}} and Lc2L_{c_{2}}, respectively. All the cycle lengths in L(c1,c2)L_{(c_{1},c_{2})} divide the length of the cycle of (z1,z2)(z_{1},z_{2}); thus, L(c1,c2)L_{(c_{1},c_{2})} contains a regular cycle. ∎

Corollary 5.1.

Finite direct product of good groups is a good group.

Proof.

Every conjugacy class in a direct product of two groups is a direct product of some of their conjugacy classes, and so any direct product of two groups is good by 5.2. Use induction to extend this to any finite direct products. ∎

Corollary 5.2.

Finite nilpotent groups are good.

Proof.

By Theorem 11 on page 113 in [14], every finite nilpotent group is a (finite) direct product of (finite) pp-groups. Every such pp-group is good by Proposition 5.1, and so is their finite direct product according to Corollary 5.1. ∎

Now we will show that 𝐒n\mathbf{S}_{n} and 𝐀n\mathbf{A}_{n} are good groups. We do it using the following proposition.

Theorem 5.1.

For any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, the group 𝐀n\mathbf{A}_{n} (resp. 𝐒n\mathbf{S}_{n}) is good.

Proof.

Let C:=Cl𝐀n⁡(e)C:=\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{A}_{n}}\left(e\right) be a conjugacy class and 𝐂:=𝐂𝐥𝐀n⁡(e)\mathbf{C}:=\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{A}_{n}}\left(e\right) a quandle for e∈Ane\in A_{n} (resp. C:=Cl𝐒n⁡(e)C:=\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{S}_{n}}\left(e\right) and 𝐂:=𝐂𝐥𝐒n⁡(e)\mathbf{C}:=\operatorname{\mathbf{Cl}}_{\mathbf{S}_{n}}\left(e\right) for e∈Sne\in S_{n}).

  • •

    If n≥5n\geq 5, then by Proposition 5.3 there is z∈{g​e​g−1∣g∈An}⊆Cz\in\left\{geg^{-1}\mid g\in A_{n}\right\}\subseteq C such that ⟨e⟩∩C𝐒n⁡(z)=𝟏\left<e\right>\cap\operatorname{C}_{\mathbf{S}_{n}}\left(z\right)=\mathbf{1}. Thus, CC is good by Corollary 4.1.

  • •

    If n≤4n\leq 4, then the element ee has to have order of at most four in 𝐀n\mathbf{A}_{n} (resp. 𝐒n\mathbf{S}_{n}). All such possible orders are powers of prime and using 5.1, we deduce that LeL_{e} contains a regular cycle. By Corollary 4.1, we deduce that CC is good.

∎

Theorem 5.2.

For any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, n≥3n\geq 3, the dihedral group 𝐃2​n\mathbf{D}_{2n} is good.

Proof.

Let Cl𝐃2​n⁡(e)\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{D}_{2n}}\left(e\right) be a conjugacy class in 𝐃2​n\mathbf{D}_{2n}. Using Corollary 4.1, to show that Cl𝐃2​n⁡(e)\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{D}_{2n}}\left(e\right) is good, it is enough to show that LeL_{e} contains a regular cycle.

By the definition of 𝐃2​n\mathbf{D}_{2n}, there are elements s,o∈D2​ns,o\in D_{2n} such that 𝐃2​n=⟨s,o∣e2=on=1&sos−1=o−1⟩\mathbf{D}_{2n}=\left<s,o\mid e^{2}=o^{n}=1\ \&\ sos^{-1}=o^{-1}\right>. Since s​o​s=s−1​o​s=s−1​o​s−1=s​o​s−1=o−1sos=s^{-1}os=s^{-1}os^{-1}=sos^{-1}=o^{-1}, it holds that D2​n⊆{sok,ok∣k∈ℤ}D_{2n}\subseteq\{so^{k},o^{k}\mid k\in\mathbb{Z}\}.

  • •

    If e=s​oke=so^{k}, then e2=(s​ok​s)​ok=o−k​ok=1e^{2}=(so^{k}s)o^{k}=o^{-k}o^{k}=1, and so the order of ee divides two. Thus, by Lemma 5.1, LeL_{e} contains a regular cycle.

  • •

    If e=oke=o^{k}, then Cl𝐃2​n(e)⊆{ϕs​ok′(e),ϕok′(e)∣k′∈ℤ}={o±k}\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathbf{D}_{2n}}\left(e\right)\subseteq\{\phi_{so^{k^{\prime}}}(e),\phi_{o^{k^{\prime}}}(e)\mid k^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}\}=\{o^{\pm k}\}. Thus, Le=1L_{e}=1 because LeL_{e} is a permutation on a set with at most two elements and it already holds that Le​(e)=eL_{e}(e)=e.

∎

In Example 3.1, we have shown that some of the good groups might define a conjugation quandle on a conjugacy class which are not connected, and yet, they have the Hayashi property. We see that finite nilpotent groups, 𝐒n,𝐀n\mathbf{S}_{n},\mathbf{A}_{n} and 𝐃2​n\mathbf{D}_{2n} are good, and we were moreover able to verify in GAP that any group of order ≤500\leq 500 and any simple nonabelian groups of order ≤3.500.000\leq 3.500.000 is good.

Problem 5.1 (Extended Hayashi’s Problem).

What groups 𝐆\mathbf{G} are good?
